core: Working definition: language development as the process by which children acquire their first language — the sounds, words, and rules of the language(s) around them
Milestone sequence: cooing, babbling, first words, telegraphic speech — each a typical range with variation, attributed to NIDCD/OpenStax
The critical-period idea: language learning is easiest in early childhood — a window of ease, not a cliff
The nature-nurture debate: Chomsky's innate capacity (Language Acquisition Device) vs learning accounts (Skinner's reinforcement, imitation) — attributed as theories
Bilingualism: learning two languages is common and normal worldwide; early mixing and uneven per-language vocabulary are typical
The honest note: every child's path is a little different — milestones are ranges, not deadlines
The honest framing: language is the mind's first great achievement
supporting: Vocabulary growth in toddlerhood (roughly 50-200 words by about age 2; up to about 1,000 by age 3)
Receptive language runs ahead of productive language
Holophrases and overextension as early word-learning phenomena
Milestones as what most children (75% or more, per CDC) can do by a given age
Caregiver interaction and child-directed speech support language growth
Interactionist accounts combining biology and social experience

claims.claim: Language development is the process by which children acquire their first language — the sounds, words, and rules of the language spoken around them; NIDCD describes language as a set of shared rules that allow people to express ideas, and OpenStax describes language development as a complex process influenced by both nature and nurture.
Children's early communication follows a typical sequence — crying, cooing, babbling, gestures, single words, then two-word phrases — with timing that varies from child to child.
Cooing — vowel-like sounds such as 'oooo' and 'ah' — typically appears by about 2 months (NIDCD lists it in the birth-to-3-months band; MedlinePlus places it at 2 to 4 months).
Babbling — repeated consonant-vowel strings such as 'mama' and 'baba' — typically begins around 4 to 6 months; early babbling is sound play without meaning, not yet real words.

Most children say their first recognizable words around their first birthday (some as early as 9 months); first words are often names for familiar people and things such as 'mama,' 'dada,' or 'dog,' and NIDCD counts one or two words by the first birthday as typical.
Telegraphic speech — short two-word combinations such as 'more cookie' that carry meaning without full grammar — typically appears between about 18 and 24 months.
Vocabulary grows rapidly in toddlerhood: roughly 50 to 200 words by about age 2 and up to about 1,000 words by age 3.

Developmental milestones are typical ranges, not deadlines: they describe what most children can do by a given age, and individual timing varies (CDC defines milestones as things most children — 75% or more — can do by a given age; NIDCD notes children vary in development while following a natural timetable).

The first three years of life are the most intensive period for acquiring speech and language skills, and there appear to be critical periods when the brain is best able to absorb language; if these periods pass without exposure, language is more difficult — but not impossible — to learn.

In the nature-nurture debate, Chomsky's nativist theory proposed an innate, uniquely human Language Acquisition Device (LAD) that predisposes us to learn language, while learning accounts — Skinner's operant conditioning of vocalizations and imitation of others — hold that language is acquired through experience; both are theories, and contemporary interactionist accounts combine biological readiness with social environment.

Children in multilingual environments learn two or more languages naturally; early mixing of languages and a temporarily smaller vocabulary in each language are normal, and fluency develops with continued exposure and support for each language; early exposure provides the greatest advantage.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How do children acquire language: innate capacity or learned behavior?
positions: Nativist view (Chomsky): humans are born with a language-ready brain, which he called a Language Acquisition Device (LAD)
Learning view (Skinner): language is acquired through operant conditioning of vocalizations, plus imitation of others
Interactionist view: biological readiness activated through social interaction
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents all three as theories, attributes each account to its theorist per OpenStax 3.5, and notes that contemporary accounts are interactionist. No position is asserted as proven fact.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How hard is the early-language window?
positions: Strong versions: language must be acquired in early childhood or it cannot be learned at all
NIDCD: the first 3 years are the most intensive period, with critical periods; passing them makes language 'more difficult to learn'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses NIDCD's wording — easier early, more difficult later — and adds the honest note that it is a window, not a cliff: adults demonstrably do learn languages throughout life.

The draft's claim that a college-level explanation 'names the concept, describes its parts, and shows how those parts work together' and its toolbox-drawer analogy were unsupported and removed.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft prose with source-verified content from NIDCD, OpenStax Lifespan Development (sections 3.5 and 5.4), MedlinePlus, and the CDC.

Milestones are presented as typical ranges with variation, per NIDCD ('children vary in their development... follow a natural progression or timetable') and the CDC (most children, 75% or more), never as absolute deadlines.
The critical-period claim was softened to NIDCD's own wording ('more difficult to learn') rather than a hard cutoff.

sourceRecords.title: Speech and Language Developmental Milestones
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD), National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Primary source for the milestone sequence (coos and pleasure sounds by 3 months; babbles in a speech-like way at 4-6 months; one or two words — 'Hi,' 'dog,' 'Dada,' 'Mama' — by the first birthday; puts two words together, e.g. 'More cookie,' at 1-2 years), for the critical-period statement (first 3 years most intensive; 'critical periods... more difficult to learn' if they pass), and for the note that children vary in development while following a natural timetable. Milestones treated as typical ranges; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 3.5: Language in Infants and Toddlers
sourceRecords.notes: OpenStax blocks direct fetch; read via web.archive.org capture web/20241105003738. Supports the working definition (language development as a complex process influenced by nature and nurture), the milestone table (cooing ~2 months; babbling 4-6 months; gesturing 7-9 months; first words and holophrases 9-12 months; telegraphic speech 16-24 months), vocabulary growth (50-200 words by ~2 years; up to 1,000 by ~3 years), overextension/underextension, and the theory review: Chomsky's LAD (nativist), Skinner's operant conditioning plus imitation (learning), and the interactionist synthesis.

sourceRecords.title: Lifespan Development, Section 5.4: Language in Early Childhood
sourceRecords.notes: Read via web.archive.org capture (2024). The 'Development in Multilingual Environments' subsection supports the bilingualism claims: children in multilingual environments learn multiple languages naturally; mixing languages and a smaller per-language vocabulary early are normal; fluency follows continued exposure; early exposure provides the greatest advantage; families in many countries (e.g., United States, Italy, Indonesia) raise multilingual children.
